title: RNAcomp2D: a web tool to execute multiple methods and visually compare predictions of RNA secondary structure.
abstract: Ribonucleic acids (RNAs) are involved in many important biological processes. In particular, non-coding RNAs are crucial regulators of cellular processes, playing a significant role in gene expression. RNA secondary structure is key to infer their specific function and for understanding how they interact with other molecules. Many computational models have been developed in the last decade to predict the secondary structure, achieving increasingly higher success rates. However, each new method has its own input-output interface, programming language, computational requirements and, sometimes, a dedicated server to run the model or just a source code in a repository. Thus, nowadays it is very hard to obtain predictions from multiple methods and compare them at once. A unified interface is urgently needed, which allows accessing several methods at the same time, visualizing and comparing predictions among them, and also with a reference structure when available. We introduce here RNAcomp2D, a web-based tool that allows users to enter an RNA sequence, or select one from RNAcentral, and obtain predictions of RNA secondary structures using several state-of-the-art methods. Both classical thermodynamic methods and the latest deep learning models are packaged in containers and accessible in an unified website. All the predictions, and the reference structure if available, are shown at the same time in a single graphical interface. Moreover, as new models continue to be developed, this tool is designed to be scalable, allowing the addition of more prediction methods in the future. Web server is available at https://sinc.unl.edu.ar/web-demo/rnacomp2d/. Data and source code are available at https://github.com/sinc-lab/RNAcomp2D. Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

title: CryoID2: deep learning-enhanced identification of protein and RNA from cryoEM maps.
abstract: Identifying the molecular components of cryoEM/cryoET maps of endogenous or poorly characterized complexes remains a major bottleneck. CryoID2 addresses this by integrating deep learning-based feature prediction with sequence prioritization and structural evaluation. Three 3D U-Nets extract structure classes, key-atom positions, and reduced residue/nucleotide types from the input map. These predictions support backbone tracing and the generation of short sequence queries that rank candidates from a user-supplied pool-using BLASTp for proteins and a maximin strategy for RNA. Corresponding PDB or AlphaFold models are then retrieved, rigidly fitted using predicted features and experimental density, and ranked by map agreement. Module-level tests show high-recall feature prediction and resolution-dependent atom clustering, while a 52-case benchmark recovers near-reference fitting quality. In practice, cryoID2 correctly identified PfA-M17 from a 166-protein mass-spectrometry pool and the unannotated Ca-raiA RNA from a genome-derived non-coding sequence set, demonstrating a unified sequence-plus-structure route to molecular identification in cryoEM maps.

title: DDX3X and DDX3Y in human reproduction and development: from molecular mechanisms to clinical implications.
abstract: DDX3X and DDX3Y are paralogous DEAD-box RNA helicases on the human sex chromosomes that share over 90% sequence identity yet act in different tissues. They have been treated as two unrelated disease genes-DDX3Y an azoospermia factor, DDX3X a neurodevelopmental one-but here we read them as paralogs that share one RNA-regulatory activity, redeployed at successive points in reproduction and development. Their shared activity is the selective translation of structured transcripts, including G-quadruplex-bearing 5 ' leaders, organised within RNA-protein condensates whose material state the two paralogs set differently. We follow this activity across gametogenesis and early development: DDX3Y in the early male germline, where loss in complete AZFa deletion gives Sertoli cell only syndrome; maternal DDX3X through oocyte maturation, the oocyte-to-embryo transition, the placenta, and corticogenesis, where loss causes the DDX3X neurodevelopmental disorder. Which paralog becomes limiting in a given tissue reflects the local balance between them, set against a shared requirement to keep their combined output within a narrow range. The narrow, near-categorical male phenotype and the graded, multisystem female one may reflect this shared activity acting at different developmental moments. What the two phenotypes share is that activity, not a common causal lesion.

title: A comparative study of quantum-inspired Gaussian Boson Sampling, dynamic programming, and machine learning methods for RNA folding prediction.
abstract: We investigate the feasibility of quantum-inspired methods for the prediction of RNA secondary structure. We further provide a comprehensive comparison and review of three major paradigms for RNA folding prediction, i.e., classical, deep learning-based, and quantum-inspired algorithms. Our results indicate that the quantum-inspired Gaussian boson sampling (GBS) approach achieves competitive structural predictions without any training requirement, exhibiting stable scaling behavior in both matched base pairs and energetic objective value as sequence length increases. While deep learning-based methods generally attain higher absolute pairing accuracy, the GBS-based formulation offers a transparent, interpretable, and data-independent alternative that effectively captures dominant folding patterns. Moreover, its simplicity and modular graph-based representation make it particularly well suited for consensus and ensemble prediction frameworks, where it can complement black-box learning models. These findings demonstrate that quantum-inspired techniques provide a promising and scalable trade-off between simplicity, interpretability, and predictive performance for RNA secondary structure prediction, particularly when used within ensemble or consensus frameworks.

title: A compact three-way junction oligonucleotide probe for widefield and super-resolution imaging of RNAs and proteins.
abstract: Molecular imaging of RNAs and proteins requires methods that preserve nanoscale organization while enabling large-scale tissue analysis. However, weak or low-abundance targets often need signal amplification, which can increase labeling size, background, or signal spread and compromise super-resolution imaging. Here, we report a compact three-way junction (3WJ) oligonucleotide probe platform for multiscale RNA and protein imaging. The design couples paired target recognition with junction assembly and recruitment of preassembled amplifier complexes, while tunable amplification balances signal strength and labeling size. Using DNA origami and single-molecule localization microscopy, we show enhanced signal while retaining the ability to resolve nanoscale target patterns. The platform improves RNA detection and supports simultaneous RNA-protein super-resolution imaging in cells. It also enhances protein detection in formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissues under low-numerical-aperture, large-field imaging conditions. Together, this programmable 3WJ platform enables sensitive RNA and protein detection across scales, supporting super-resolution analysis of molecular organization and large-field tissue mapping.

title: Aging Remodels the Female Skeletal Muscle Proteome Toward Matrix, Chromatin and Lysosomal Programs that Track Loss of Physical Function.
abstract: Loss of skeletal muscle strength and mobility is among the most consequential features of human aging, yet the molecular programs that accompany this decline in women remain poorly understood. Here, we performed deep comprehensive data-independent acquisition (DIA) proteomic profiling of vastus lateralis biopsies from 10 younger (24-30 years) and 10 older (70-84 years) healthy women enrolled through the NIH Common Fund Cellular Senescence Network (SenNet), with matched measurements of grip strength and gait speed. Of 2,391 quantified protein groups, 163 were significantly altered with age, and partial least squares-discriminant analysis completely separated the age groups (cross-validated AUC = 1.00). Older muscle showed increased extracellular matrix and vascular remodeling proteins (TIMP3, COL8A1, ELN, FBN1), nuclear, chromatin and RNA-binding proteins (HMGB1, HMGB2, histone H1.0, MATR3, NCL), and lysosomal and senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP)-associated proteins (CTSZ, CTSD, PSAP), together with reduced glycolytic and energetic proteins (GAPDH, ENO3, PHKA1, CYCS). Age effects were robust to adjust for body mass index (BMI). Integrating differential abundance, multivariate importance and participant-level consistency, we defined a 24-protein skeletal muscle aging signature whose score separated all younger from all elderly women. Combining grip strength and gait speed into a combined function score, we found that 23 of the 24 signature proteins correlated with physical function (FDR < 0.05), and the signature score correlated strongly with function (r = -0.79). The senescence-associated alarmins HMGB1 and HMGB2 emerged as lead proteins: HMGB1 showed the strongest association with function (r = -0.86), and both remained associated after adjustment for age group. Together, these data define a senotype proteomic program in aging female skeletal muscle and a molecular signature of muscle function that, after validation, may serve as a readout for interventions that aim to preserve physical performance in elderly women.

title: A global post-transcriptional regulator directs Acinetobacter baumannii carbon preference and gut colonization.
abstract: Acinetobacter baumannii is a multidrug-resistant pathogen that colonizes the gut, increasing the risk of subsequent infection and transmission. Recent work showed that A. baumannii catabolizes ornithine, a non-preferred carbon source, to colonize the gut. However, the mechanisms of carbon preference were unknown in A. baumannii . Here, experimental evolution identified the conserved RNA-binding protein CsrA as a regulator of carbon preference in A. baumannii , a previously unreported CsrA function. RNA immunoprecipitation sequencing (RIP-Seq) revealed hundreds of CsrA-bound transcripts . A. baumannii CsrA directly bound and repressed expression of the ast arginine/ornithine catabolic operons. The Pseudomonas aeruginosa CsrA homolog RsmA repressed arginine/ornithine catabolic operon expression, suggesting this CsrA function extends to other bacterial taxa. Finally, CsrA was required for competitive fitness during A. baumannii gut colonization. These findings uncover a previously unrecognized role for a global regulator in A. baumannii carbon preference and persistence in the gut, a critical reservoir for multidrug-resistant pathogens.

title: Engineering Synthetic Molecular Operations Controlled by DNA-Binding Proteins Through Templated Proximity.
abstract: We describe a DNA-based molecular framework that enables DNA-binding proteins (DBPs) to perform diverse synthetic operations beyond their natural functions. We introduce templated proximity as a mechanism through which DBP-DNA recognition events are converted into programmable DNA strand displacement reactions. In this architecture, protein binding templates the spatial colocalization of split DNA components, generating functional nucleic acid outputs that can be propagated into downstream processes. Using representative DBPs, including EGR1, YY1, and p53, we couple protein recognition to DNA strand displacement, activation of a fluorogenic RNA aptamer, regulation of CRISPR-Cas12a and Cas13 activity, and DBP-triggered activation of hierarchical CRISPR cascades. These results establish templated proximity as a general transduction principle for integrating DNA-binding proteins into modular nucleic acid reaction networks and demonstrate that DBPs can function as programmable interfaces connecting natural biomolecular recognition with engineered DNA-based information processing, enabling modular communication layers with tailored synthetic functionality.

title: Ionic condition-dependent allostery shapes ribosomal dynamics.
abstract: Ionic composition is a key determinant of ribosomal RNA structure and function. Metal cations such as potassium (K+) and magnesium (Mg2+) stabilize rRNA architecture. While certain positions in the ribosome are strictly occupied by either potassium or magnesium for distinct structural or functional reasons, their broader role in modulating ribosomal dynamics remains poorly understood. Here, we use microsecond-scale coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations of the bacterial 70S ribosome to examine how ionic composition affects structural flexibility and long-range communication. We compare a native ribosome with experimentally resolved ions to two variants: a magnesium-enriched model, in which K+ ions are replaced with Mg2+, and a hydrated magnesium model. While these substitutions do not aim to reproduce physiological ionic conditions, they provide a controlled framework to isolate the physical effects of ion identity on ribosomal dynamics. Increasing magnesium content reduces ionic and backbone mobility and enhances rigidity within the ribosomal core. Dynamic Flexibility Index analysis shows that these changes extend beyond local coordination sites, producing flexibility shifts at distances exceeding 30 Å. Dynamic Coupling Index analysis further reveals that ionic perturbations reshape long-range communication pathways. Functionally important regions, including the L1 and L7/12 stalks, exhibit distinct, ion-dependent responses, while the L10-L11 region shows enhanced long-range coupling under varying ionic conditions. These results demonstrate that ionic composition modulates both local stability and global ribosomal dynamics, with implications for translational efficiency and fidelity.

title: Variant Classification of a Non-Protein Coding Gene: ACMG/AMP Specifications for RMRP from the Clinical Genome Resource Severe Combined Immunodeficiency Disease Variant Curation Expert Panel.
abstract: This study, conducted by the Clinical Genome Resource Severe Combined Immunodeficiency Disease Variant Curation Expert Panel (ClinGen SCID-VCEP), aimed to adapt the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics/Association for Molecular Pathology (ACMG/AMP) framework for germline variant interpretation in RMRP . Unlike the protein-coding genes for which the framework was primarily developed, RMRP encodes a non-protein-coding RNA. Biallelic pathogenic variants in RMRP cause cartilage-hair hypoplasia, which can include severe combined immunodeficiency disease and other immune abnormalities. An RMRP -focused SCID-VCEP subgroup reviewed all 28 ACMG/AMP evidence criteria using population databases, published clinical and experimental data, computational predictions, and expert consensus. Each criterion was retained, modified, or designated as not applicable based on RMRP biology and disease mechanisms. The resulting specifications were pilot tested using 27 variants selected from ClinVar and research laboratory data. Fifteen ACMG/AMP criteria were determined to be applicable to RMRP , while 13 were considered not applicable. Several criteria were modified to evaluate nucleotide-level effects on transcriptional regulation, critical promoter regions, and RNA secondary structure. The specifications also incorporated RMRP -specific recommendations for population frequency, functional evidence, variant phase, segregation, and phenotype. Application of the specifications classified 6 variants as pathogenic, 10 as likely pathogenic, 7 as variants of uncertain significance, and 4 as benign. Previously pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants remained within the pathogenic spectrum, and all previously benign variants remained benign. Variants with conflicting ClinVar interpretations were resolved as either likely pathogenic or uncertain. PM1, PM3, and PP4 were the primary criteria supporting pathogenic classifications. The SCID-VCEP specifications provide a standardized approach to the classification of germline RMRP variants in cartilage-hair hypoplasia and demonstrate how the ACMG/AMP framework can be adapted for a disease-associated non-protein-coding RNA gene. These specifications support the development of variant interpretation frameworks for other clinically relevant non-protein-coding genes.

title: SlitOBP9 contributes to cis-3-hexenol recognition and larval orientation in Spodoptera litura.
abstract: Cis-3-hexenol is a typical green leaf volatile (GLV) that plays an important regulatory role in plant-insect interactions. Spodoptera litura is a globally significant agricultural pest whose larvae cause severe damage to a wide range of crops, yet the olfactory molecular mechanism underlying larval recognition of this volatile has remained unclear. Two-choice behavioral assays showed that a low dose (0.1 µg) of cis-3-hexenol exerted a significant attractive effect on S. litura larvae. Tissue-specific expression analysis identified an odorant-binding protein, SlitOBP9, that is highly expressed in the larval antennae. Fluorescence competitive binding assays confirmed that SlitOBP9 binds cis-3-hexenol, with the highest binding affinity at neutral pH (7.4); binding capacity was lost under acidic (pH 5.0) or alkaline (pH 9.0) conditions. RNA interference (RNAi)-mediated silencing of SlitOBP9 significantly reduced larval chemotactic behavior toward cis-3-hexenol. Relative to siNC controls, siOBP9-injected larvae showed a marked decrease in food intake on maize and cabbage, together with highly significant reductions in body-weight gain, and frass production. These results indicate that SlitOBP9 contributes to the perception of cis-3-hexenol and provide a systematic account of the olfactory mechanism by which S. litura larvae recognize this ecologically important volatile. These findings may provide a basic mechanistic lead for future studies, but further work is needed before any practical pest-control application can be considered.

title: Fatty Acid Synthase Binds Cellular mRNAs and its Depletion Reduces Translational Efficiency.
abstract: Metabolic enzymes with non-canonical RNA binding activity have drawn a growing interest, due to their implications for basic biology and disease. Here we present the first RNA interactome of fatty acid synthase (FASN), an emerging oncological and virological target. Utilizing crosslinking-based approaches, we characterize the direct RNA association of FASN in two human cell lines, identifying over 6000 binding sites across over 3500 protein-coding genes, with a striking preference for the 5' UTR. We provide a functional cross-screen on the effects of FASN depletion on cellular translation. This integration with ribosome profiling indicated a preferential reduction in the translational efficiencies of FASN-associated mRNAs - an effect shown to be dependent on binding location and site number. Associated transcripts were enriched for morphogenic and cell division-related functions, as well as palmitoylated proteins. Together, these findings identify a transcript-selective, position-dependent relationship between FASN RNA binding and translation, expanding the cellular functions attributable to this metabolic enzyme.

title: Deducing splicing events from transcript sets with splicelogic.
abstract: Long-read RNA sequencing captures a greater proportion of full-length transcripts, enabling more accurate isoform identification, discovery of novel isoforms, and more precise differential transcript usage analysis. However, comparing transcripts, whether between conditions or between sets such as novel and annotated isoforms, yields complex isoform changes that are hard to manipulate, summarize, and visualize. This is compounded by vertical integration of some tools, where downstream analysis depends on the specific output of a particular upstream tool. To address this gap, we have developed splicelogic, an R/Bioconductor package that makes transcript-set comparisons biologically interpretable by turning them into discrete splicing events, such as exon skipping, alternative splice sites, intron retention, and alternative transcription start and end sites. We designed splicelogic to integrate easily with existing RNA-seq workflows and tools. The splicelogic functions are modular, readable, and extensible, making it easy for users to adapt core logic to their own custom scientific questions or novel splicing definitions. By obtaining interpretable splicing events from transcript changes, splicelogic enables downstream analyses, including annotation of RNA-binding protein recognition sites, alongside summary statistics and visualization. The splicelogic package is publicly available and distributed through Bioconductor.

title: Conserved RNA structural elements mediate WDR5 recognition of the long non-coding RNA UMLILO.
abstract: The long non-coding RNA (lncRNA), UMLILO (upstream master lncRNA of the inflammatory chemokine locus), regulates the epigenetic programming of innate immune genes. Although its basic mechanism was revealed in cells, the molecular basis by which UMLILO interacts with its partner, WD repeat-containing protein 5 (WDR5), remained unknown. To understand how UMLILO interacts with WDR5, we determined the secondary structure of UMLILO by chemical probing and performed binding assays, uncovering the multivalent nature of their interaction, involving multiple RNA stem-loops. Conservational analysis revealed a stem-loop structurally conserved across mammals. Furthermore, we found that UMLILO engages multiple sites on the surface of WDR5 as revealed by NMR chemical shift perturbation analysis, and that full-length UMLILO increases WDR5 recruitment into in vitro condensates. Our report provides a detailed characterization of the molecular basis of WDR5 recognition by an RNA and establishes a new paradigm for the role of IPLs in enhancing gene expression.

title: Characterization and comparative analysis of the complete mitochondrial genome of Christia vespertilionis (Leguminosae: Desmodieae).
abstract: Christia vespertilionis, a legume species commonly known as "butterfly wings" or "aircraft grass", holds considerable ornamental and medicinal values. It belongs to the taxonomically challenging tribe Desmodieae within the non-protein amino acid accumulating (NPAAA) clade of Fabaceae. Although its chloroplast genome has been documented, the mitochondrial genome remains uncharacterized, thereby hindering our comprehensive understanding of its genomic structure and evolutionary dynamics. In this study, we employed Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT) and Illumina sequencing data to assemble and annotate the complete mitochondrial genome of C. vespertilionis. The mitochondrial genome is circular, spanning 423,055 bp, and contains a total of 52 annotated genes, including 33 protein-coding genes (PCGs), 16 tRNA genes, and three rRNA genes. We detected 503 potential editing events across 32 of the 33 mitochondrial PCGs, with the nad4 and ccmB genes showing the highest editing frequencies. Comparative genomic analyses revealed that the mt genomes are conserved within tribe Desmodieae in terms of gene composition, codon preference and RNA editing patterns, suggesting functional evolutionary constraints. However, notable differences were observed in the patterns of repetitive sequences and mitochondrial plastid DNAs (MTPTs), indicating evolutionary dynamics. Specifically, C. vespertilionis contains 299 dispersed repeats (DRs) and 102 SSRs, whereas its relative Hylodesmum podocarpum harbors 472 DRs and 139 SSRs. Both species possess 18 MTPTs, with total lengths of 3450 bp in C. vespertilionis and 3154 bp in H. podocarpum. MTPTs shorter than 100 bp share the same tRNA flanking regions distribution, whereas those exceeding 100 bp exhibit distinct distribution patterns. Phylogenetic analyses based on concatenated datasets of shared mitochondrial and chloroplast PCGs generated an identical topology with high resolution at the tribe level. Within the NPAAA clade, 22 species from 10 tribes were resolved into two monophyletic subclades. The tribe Desmodieae, represented by C. vespertilionis and H. podocarpum, was well-supported as a monophyletic sister group to the tribe Phaseoleae. In this study, we sequenced, assembled, and annotated the mitochondrial genome of C. vespertilionis for the first time and conducted comparative genomic and phylogenetic analyses with species from the NPAAA clade. Our findings contribute to the mitochondrial genome database of legume plants and provide valuable insights into the exploitation and utilization of C. vespertilionis, as well as for taxonomic and evolutionary investigations within the taxonomically tribe Desmodieae.

title: An atlas of the sRNAs and their targets in Staphylococcus aureus
abstract: Staphylococcus aureus is an opportunistic pathogen that causes various diseases in animals and humans. Small RNAs (sRNAs) control major steps in the infection process and acclimation responses, contributing to the architecture of the regulatory networks. However, a large number of putative sRNAs remain poorly characterized. Here we present aureoRNA, an interactive database (https://aurorna.biologie.uni-freiburg.de) that integrates available information for each sRNA, including phylogeny in the phylum Bacillota, public transcriptome datasets for sRNA and mRNA correlation, and permits computational predictions of sRNA functions. The aureoRNA-based analysis of the sRNA RsaD revealed new targets including the oxidative threonine catabolism and the arginine deiminase pathway. A target-centric search identifying potential sRNAs for mRNAs of interest revealed the citZ citrate synthase mRNA as an RsaE target, and two small prophage genes as RNAIII interaction partner. The aureoRNA database facilitates the functional characterization of the entire set of sRNAs and their targets in this major pathogen.

title: FusionGDB 3.0: integrating breakpoints, generating personalized sequences, and inferring tumorigenic scenarios for human fusion genes.
abstract: FusionGDB has served diverse biological, health, and clinical research communities as a unique functional annotation knowledgebase of human fusion genes. In this study, we report an updated resource of human fusion gene annotation (FusionGDB 3.0), available at https://compbio.uth.edu/FusionGDB/. FusionGDB 3.0 includes substantial content updates: 156K up-to-date human fusion genes established by integrating 216K RNA-seq-based and 100K WGS-based breakpoint events, comprehensive open reading frame annotations, protein domain retention searches, and 1.13 million personalized fusion protein sequences reflecting individual nsSNVs from TCGA and CCLE, as well as N- and C-truncated protein sequences alongside canonical in-frame products. Furthermore, it incorporates 18K potential tumorigenic scenarios, supported by evidence from the literature, spanning drug-targetable gene group fusions, the epigenomic architecture around breakpoint junctions, and therapeutic prioritization scoring. FusionGDB 3.0 establishes a systematic framework for the functional annotation of coding structural variants. FusionGDB 3.0 serves as a pivotal reference knowledgebase for the genomics, oncology, and precision pharmacology communities, while also functioning as a foundational benchmark dataset for training and validating machine learning models, structural biology platforms, and AI-driven therapeutic discovery pipelines.

title: SAM-Dependent Precursor Peptide Engagement by Darobactin Maturase DarE
abstract: Radical S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) enzymes that synthesize structurally constrained ribosomally synthesized and post-translationally modified peptides (RiPPs) with therapeutic potential mostly do so by employing a dedicated RiPP recognition element (RRE). With the growing number of RRE-free maturases discovered, how these enzymes engage their substrates remains largely unexplored. In this work, we mapped substrate-enzyme interactions in DarE, an RRE-free radical SAM enzyme that installs the C-C and C-O-C crosslinks of the antibiotic darobactin during the first step of darobactin biosynthesis. Using anaerobic hydrogen-deuterium exchange mass spectrometry (HDX-MS), we simultaneously resolved specific regions within the enzyme and its precursor peptide substrate, DarA, across five complex states. The N-terminal extension and part of the TIM-barrel domain of DarE, along with the leader region of DarA, become protected, revealing the peptide-engagement interface. Additional protection emerged only in the presence of SAM, identifying SAM as a key contributor to precursor-peptide engagement in an RRE-free RiPP maturase. Electron paramagnetic resonance spectroscopy further demonstrated precursor peptide-dependent perturbations of the chemical environment of the iron-sulfur clusters. These findings suggest that SAM-dependent peptide engagement, mediated in part by the N-terminal extension of the radical SAM enzyme, provides an alternative mechanism for precursor-peptide recognition in RRE-free RiPP maturases. Our work also demonstrates the utility of anaerobic HDX-MS for characterizing protein-peptide-small molecule interactions in oxygen-sensitive metalloenzymes.

title: Anti-HER-2-modified exosomes loaded with siRNA-STIL specifically target and inhibit the development and progression of gastric cancer.
abstract: STIL is a key molecule influencing the proliferation and cell cycle of gastric cancer cells; however, STIL is also expressed in normal tissues. Therefore, designing a drug delivery system that targets gastric cancer cells is crucial for STIL-targeted therapy. In this study, we constructed exosomes targeting the HER-2 receptor and loaded with siSTIL (Anti-HER-2-Exo-siSTIL), and validated the inhibitory effects of Anti-HER-2-Exo-siSTIL on gastric cancer proliferation and metastasis in vivo. Anti-HER-2-Exo-siSTIL was able to enter SGC-7901 cells and inhibit STIL expression, significantly suppressing the growth of SGC-7901 xenograft tumors. By downregulating STIL and the anti-apoptotic protein Bcl-2, and upregulating the pro-apoptotic proteins Bax, Caspase-3, and Caspase-9, Anti-HER-2-Exo-siSTIL effectively induced apoptosis in tumor cells. Furthermore, Anti-HER-2-Exo-siSTIL selectively inhibited lung metastasis of SGC-7901 cells via hematogenous dissemination. In summary, Anti-HER-2-Exo-siSTIL specifically targets and suppresses gastric cancer proliferation and lung metastasis, demonstrating its significant translational potential for gastric cancer therapy.

title: Integration of lncRNA-miRNA-target regulatory axis in natural products and radiation responses.
abstract: The lncRNA-miRNA-mRNA-protein regulatory axis is a key determinant of cellular responses to ionizing radiation, yet studies typically treat radiation-responsive long noncoding RNA (lncRNA), microRNAs (miRNAs), downstream mRNA (transcript) targets and their encoded proteins, and bioactive natural products in isolation. To bridge this gap, the aim on this review was to combine radiation-modulated lncRNAs, miRNAs, and explicitly annotated mRNA and corresponding proteins with natural compounds that exhibit radiosensitizing, radioprotective, and anticancer activities. Radiation-responsive lncRNAs, miRNAs, and their mRNA/protein targets were compiled and curated; functional lncRNA-miRNA-mRNA-protein regulatory axes reconstructed; and how these axes coordinate diverse cellular processes following radiation mapped. Thirty-three natural products that concurrently influenced radiosensitization, radioprotection, and tumor suppression were prioritized and linked to specific axes to determine shared molecular mechanisms. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) issued Generally Recognized as Safe (GRAS) "no questions" responses for astaxanthin, curcumin, fucoidan, lycopene, and quercetin were examined in support of safety and translational potential. A total of 399 articles were retrieved from Google Scholar for review period 2001-2026. Using bioinformatics tool STRING, protein-protein interaction network of encoded targets analyzed, indicating hubs and pathway convergence points amenable to pharmacologic modulation. By overlaying natural product effects onto reconstructed axes, candidate trifunctional natural products were nominated that regulate radiation responses via lncRNA modulation, miRNA sponging, and direct regulation of mRNAs and/or their encoded proteins. In conclusion, this review demonstrates the potential of high‑value natural products to enhance radiation responses via lncRNA-miRNA-mRNA-protein networks.

title: Exosome-inspired biomimetic nanocarriers: Biological principles, fabrication strategies, characterization, and therapeutic applications.
abstract: Biomimetic nanocarriers inspired by exosomes have emerged as a transformative strategy for precision drug delivery by combining the biological advantages of naturally derived extracellular vesicles with the scalability and tunability of synthetic nanotechnology. Native exosomes exhibit intrinsic immune evasion, membrane stability, ligand-mediated cellular tropism, and the ability to traverse complex biological barrier properties that conventional nanocarriers have struggled to replicate. This review systematically discusses the biological basis of exosomes, including their biogenesis, molecular composition, and intercellular communication roles, and translates these principles into engineering strategies for designing exosome-inspired biomimetic nanocarriers. We critically examine major biomimetic platforms such as cell membrane-coated nanoparticles, hybrid exosome-synthetic vesicles, lipid-based exosome mimetics, and polymeric biomimetic assemblies, with emphasis on fabrication techniques, drug loading approaches, targeting mechanisms, and advanced characterization methods. Recent therapeutic applications across oncology, central nervous system disorders, immunotherapy, gene and RNA delivery, and regenerative medicine are summarised with comparative insights into mechanistic performance. Furthermore, key challenges related to safety, manufacturing scalability, regulatory considerations, and quality control are discussed. Emerging trends, including microfluidic manufacturing, quality-by-design frameworks, and artificial intelligence-assisted nanocarrier optimization, are highlighted as future directions. Finally, we outline critical research gaps and propose a translational roadmap for clinical development of exosome-inspired biomimetic nanocarriers.

title: The ErbB4 Agonist JK07 Attenuates Heart Failure-Related Gene Expression and Activates Reparative Cardiac Pathways in a Murine HFrEF Model.
abstract: Selective activation of the neuregulin-1 (NRG-1)/ErbB pathway is a promising strategy for cardiac repair in heart failure (HF), but recombinant NRG-1 therapies are limited by poor stability and nonselective receptor activation. JK07 is a novel biologic that combines the epidermal growth factor-like domain of NRG-1 with an ErbB3-antagonist antibody, enabling preferential ErbB4 activation. In a murine myocardial infarction-induced HF model (left ventricular ejection fraction <40%), mice received single or repeated doses of JK07 (1 mg/kg) or vehicle. Cardiac structure and cellular responses were assessed using echocardiography, histology, and single-nucleus RNA sequencing. JK07 reduced interstitial fibrosis and increased capillary density while inducing robust, transient, cell-specific transcriptional responses, most pronounced 1 day after treatment. Cardiomyocytes showed enhanced ErbB4 expression and metabolic pathways, fibroblasts adopted reparative phenotypes, and endothelial cells exhibited transient angiogenic activation. JK07 also preserved mitochondrial respiration in cardiomyocytes under inflammatory stress, supporting ErbB4 activation as a potential therapeutic strategy for HF.

title: LONP-1 deficiency causes dysregulated protein synthesis within mitochondria that is suppressed by mitoribosomal mutations.
abstract: Mitochondrial homeostasis is maintained by molecular chaperones and proteases located within the organelle. The mitochondrial matrix-localized protease LONP-1 degrades oxidatively damaged or misfolded proteins. Importantly, LONP-1 also regulates mitochondrial DNA replication. Here, we show that mutations in C. elegans that impair LONP-1 function cause dysregulation of mitochondrial DNA replication, mitochondrial RNA transcription and protein synthesis within the mitochondrial matrix. LONP-1 deficient worms had reduced levels of oxidative phosphorylation proteins despite increased mtDNA-encoded protein synthesis. Via a forward genetic screen, we identified three mutations that restored mitochondrial function and the rate of development in lonp-1 mutants to levels comparable to those in wildtype worms. Interestingly, all three suppressor mutations were found in genes encoding mitochondrial ribosome proteins. A point mutation in the mitochondrial ribosome protein MRPS-38 restored oxidative phosphorylation in lonp-1 mutant worms. Combined, our results suggest that LONP-1 regulates mitochondrial translation and that suppressor mutations within mrps-38 or mrps-15 can enhance oxidative phosphorylation complex assembly when LONP-1 function is diminished.

title: A new therapeutic opportunity in Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever: Targeting the stalk domain of viral nucleocapsid protein for therapeutic intervention.
abstract: Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus (CCHFV) is a high-consequence pathogen for which no approved antivirals or vaccines exist. The viral nucleocapsid protein (N protein) is central to the Nairovirus life cycle, coordinating genomic RNA encapsidation and selective enhancement of viral mRNA translation through its interaction with the panhandle-like hairpin structure in the S-segment mRNA 5' untranslated region (UTR). Here, we developed a robust fluorescence polarization anisotropy (FPA) based high-throughput assay capable of quantitatively monitoring the interaction between purified N protein and the viral 5'UTR hairpin. The assay demonstrated excellent stability, DMSO tolerance, and performance metrics (average Z' > 0.6), enabling the screening of 108,947 small molecules. Primary screening identified 122 inhibitors, 86 of which showed clear dose-responsive activity. Cluster analysis, medicinal chemistry filtering, and repurchase-based validation yielded 37 confirmed hits, from which compounds 11, 14, and 33 were prioritized for further testing. Biochemical analysis demonstrated that all three compounds noncompetitively inhibit N protein-UTR binding with IC₅₀ values of 11-41 μM. These compounds exhibited minimal cytotoxicity (CC₅₀ > 1-2 mM) and potent antiviral activity in cell culture against Hazara virus (HZV), a BSL-2 surrogate for CCHFV, with EC₅₀ values of ~23-51 μM and favorable selectivity indices (>34-86). Plaque assays further showed that compounds 11 and 14 reduced the production of infectious viral particles by over 100-fold, whereas compound 33 nearly eliminated detectable infectious virus in the media. Mechanistic assays revealed that these inhibitors act during post-entry steps and selectively block the N protein-mediated enhancement of viral mRNA translation without affecting the canonical host translation machinery. Molecular modeling and biochemical/translation assays support binding of compound 11 to the N protein stalk-head interface, involving residues Gln300, Glu240 and Lys473. Collectively, these findings identify the N protein-5'UTR interface as a tractable antiviral target and establish first-in-class small-molecule inhibitors that disrupt essential Nairovirus RNA-N protein interaction. These compounds provide strong leads for further optimization and development of urgently needed therapeutics for CCHFV.

title: Moss is more: The moss Physcomitrium patens as an ideal chassis for plant synthetic biology.
abstract: Physcomitrium patens, commonly known as the spreading earthmoss or Physco, has gained increasing attention as a chassis for synthetic biology in plants. This review explores its advantages over flowering plants traditionally used more often for biotechnology, such as Arabidopsis thaliana and maize, including shorter life cycles and ease to handle experimentally, being haploid, and much higher efficiency for integration of transgenes into its genome by homologous recombination. In addition, Physco's ability to maintain episomes also introduces an additional possibility for transgene expression and manipulation. With these advantageous traits, Physco has already been used for synthetic genomes, recombinant protein production, metabolic engineering and artificial organelle engineering. These applications have been enabled by various toolkits developed for construction of transformation cassettes, DNA and RNA editing, as well as different reporters to allow microscopy imaging or quantification of gene expression. While Physco does have limitations, such as its high number of duplicated genes which can present issues when tweaking of native genes is involved, these certainly do not prevent Physco becoming a useful synthetic biology model for further applications on Earth and future space explorations.

title: APY0201 inhibits cell invasion and stemness, and induces ferroptosis of esophageal cancer through downregulating METTL16 to affect ALOX5 m6A methylation.
abstract: APY0201 is a phosphatidylinositol kinase containing an FYVE finger structure (PIKfyve) inhibitor that has been reported to inhibit the malignant progression of several cancers. N6-methyladenosine (m6A) methylation is the most abundant RNA modification in cancer development, including esophageal cancer (EC). This study aimed to investigate whether APY0201 played an anti-tumor role in EC, and whether its function was associated with m6A methylation. Cell viability, apoptosis, invasion, and stemness were determined using MTT assay, flow cytometry, transwell assay, and sphere formation assay for cell stemness. Ferroptosis was assessed by detecting the associated indicators. The mRNA and protein expression were examined using real-time quantitative PCR and Western blot. Methylated RNA immunoprecipitation (MeRIP) assay was performed to affirm m6A modification of ALOX5 by METTL16. RIP assay and dual-luciferase reporter assay were used to indicate the interaction between METTL16 and ALOX5. Xenograft tumor assay was conducted to explore APY0201 function in vivo. In EC cells, APY0201 suppressed cell viability, invasion, and stemness, and promoted ferroptosis by regulating arachidonate 5-lipoxygenase (ALOX5). Methyltransferase-like 16 (METTL16) catalyzed m6A methylation to affect ALOX5 mRNA stability. Functionally, METTL16 facilitated EC cell development and inhibited ferroptosis via downregulating ALOX5. Additionally, METTL16 overexpression could partly attenuate the repression role of APY0201 treatment on ALOX5 expression in EC cells. In vivo, APY0201 also reduced tumor growth by targeting the METTL16/ALOX5 axis. These functional studies demonstrate that APY0201 impeded cell malignant behaviors and induced ferroptosis in EC through METTL16-mediated ALOX5 m6A methylation.

title: Integrative analysis of keratin 14/5 expression, genetic variation, and predicted interactions associated with sheep horn phenotypes.
abstract: Keratin 14 (KRT14) and keratin 5 (KRT5), key components of epidermal keratinization, may contribute to horn-related keratinized tissues. We integrated RNA sequencing, whole-genome sequencing, allele-specific expression analysis, cross-species comparison, and protein structure prediction to examine KRT14 and KRT5 in sheep with scurred horns (SCU) and spiral or horizontally extended horns (SHE). In the limma analysis, KRT14 showed 2.30-fold higher expression in SCU than in SHE (nominal P = 0.013); however, this difference did not remain significant after Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment (adjusted P = 0.319). KRT5 showed the same direction of change, but the limma result was not significant (log2 fold change = -0.56; nominal P = 0.128; adjusted P = 0.565). Variant analysis identified 58 variants, and read-count inspection highlighted 19 preliminary candidate sites with apparent allelic read-count imbalances in the KRT14 region. Cross-species expression patterns provided descriptive context, and structural modeling predicted possible interaction interfaces among KRT14, KRT5, and receptor-interacting protein kinase 4 (RIPK4). Together, these results identify phenotype-associated expression patterns, candidate differentiated variants, and predicted protein interactions for future experimental validation; they do not establish causal mechanisms of horn morphology.

title: Photo-Activatable RNA Switches for Optical Control of Cell-Free Protein Synthesis.
abstract: Programmable RNA switches enable target-dependent regulation of cell-free protein synthesis. Here, we report a photo-activatable RNA switch using photocleavable Lock DNA (pcl-Lock) to enable optical control of in vitro translation. Synthesized by solid-phase methods, pcl-Lock incorporates a coumarin-based photocleavable linker that maintains the RNA switch in an inactive state. Irradiation with 456 nm light cleaves the linker, releasing inhibition and activating translation. Light-triggered activation produced β-galactosidase, yielding approximately 4-fold and 30-fold increases in fluorescence and glucose signals, respectively. Native polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis confirms efficient photocleavage of the pcl-Lock strand, while control experiments verify that light-dependent activation does not occur with the Lock strand lacking the photocleavable linker. This strategy enables optical regulation of cell-free protein synthesis and establishes a strategy for integrating photochemical control with programmable gene regulation.

title: Small RNA-mediated genome silencing in Caenorhabditis elegans promotes telomere stability in the absence of telomerase.
abstract: We previously found that small RNAs with perfect homology to (TTAGGC)n telomere repeats are very rare. Here we use long read sequencing to reveal that most N2 wild type C. elegans strains have few telomere mutations at 5' ends of telomeres, where the telomeric lncRNA TERRA is transcribed. Therefore, telomere mutations cannot explain the absence of perfect small RNAs to (TTAGGC)n telomere repeats. We show that the heterochromatin mark H3K9me2 is enriched at C. elegans sub-telomeres and that the HP1 protein HPL-2 that binds H3K9me2 promotes telomere stability in the absence of telomerase. Small RNA silencing can promote H3K9 methylation, and telomere stability in the absence of telomerase requires germ granule proteins MUT-7 and MUT-14 that promote small RNA biogenesis and also WAGO-1 and HRDE-1 Argonaute proteins that bind subtelomeric small RNAs. Loss of telomerase induced biogenesis of small RNAs from the subtelomeric 5' end of the telomeric lncRNA TERRA but not from telomere repeats of TERRA. Loss of both telomerase and small RNA-mediated genome silencing induced TERRA expression, telomere damage and accelerated sterility. We propose that small RNA-mediated heterochromatin formation and telomerase function redundantly to repress a form of telomeric DNA damage that is coupled to TERRA expression and subtelomeric small RNA biogenesis. However, telomere repeats of TERRA strongly resisted RNA-dependent RNA polymerase activity in telomerase mutants, revealing an exceptional quality of telomere repeat RNA.

title: Translational nanotechnology for precision gene therapy delivery systems.
abstract: Gene therapy is one of the breakthrough strategies for treating genetically acquired and complicated disorders owing to its potential in regulating the expression of genes precisely. Nevertheless, the success of any gene therapy will depend upon the development of a safe and efficient system for gene delivery. Nanotechnology has brought about great changes in the field of non-viral gene delivery systems by providing carriers that increase stability, facilitate cellular uptake, allow endosomal escape, and have tissue specificity without causing systemic toxicity. This review examines the basic concepts underlying the design of nanocarriers for the delivery of plasmid DNA, mRNA, siRNA, and the CRISPR-Cas genome editing system. The current review provides an overview of different viral and non-viral delivery platforms for plasmid DNA, mRNA, siRNA, and CRISPR-Cas genome editing systems. The discussion focuses on adenoviral, adeno-associated viral, lentiviral, retroviral, herpes simplex viral and virus-like particle delivery platforms, as well as non-viral nanocarriers. The review further highlights clinically validated examples, such as liposomal nanoparticles used for the delivery of RNA-based therapies and discusses some of the translational challenges that still exist in terms of transfection efficiency, long-term safety issues, manufacturability at a large scale, and regulatory acceptance. Finally, some of the latest trends in gene delivery, such as artificial intelligence-assisted nanoparticle design, smart multi-responsive nanoparticles, and personalized nanomedicine, have been outlined as the most important driving forces in developing the next generation of gene delivery technologies.

title: The first mitochondrial genome assembly of Ardisia gigantifolia Stapf: genome characterization, RNA editing, and phylogenetic analysis.
abstract: Ardisia gigantifolia Stapf, belonging to the genus Ardisia (Primulaceae), is an important traditional medicinal plant with extensive applications in folk medicine. However, its mitochondrial genome remains unexplored. The first mitochondrial genome of A. gigantifolia was sequenced using Illumina NovaSeq 6000 and Oxford Nanopore Technologies platforms and assembled using a hybrid strategy implemented in Unicycler. The genome was assembled into a 639,756 bp circular configuration with a GC content of 42.02%. ONT long reads supported the contig connections within this configuration, although alternative configurations may also exist. The mitochondrial genome contained 38 protein-coding genes, 20 tRNA genes, and 3 rRNA genes. Repetitive sequence analysis identified abundant repeat elements, including 63 simple sequence repeats, 62 tandem repeats, and 73 dispersed repeat regions, which may contribute to mitochondrial genome expansion and structural complexity. In addition, 72 mitochondrial plastid DNA fragments were identified between the mitochondrial and plastid genomes. A total of 451 C-to-U RNA editing sites were predicted across 38 protein-coding genes using Deepred-Mt. Fourteen editing sites in nad4L, including the conversion of its ACG start codon to AUG, and a stop-codon editing site in ccmFC were experimentally validated. Phylogenetic analysis supported a close relationship between A. gigantifolia and Aegiceras corniculatum. This study reports the first mitochondrial genome of A. gigantifolia, providing a valuable genomic resource for understanding mitochondrial genome evolution, phylogenetic relationships, and molecular characteristics of Ardisia.

title: Isolation and Genome Annotation of MamaT, a Cluster GI Bacteriophage with Podovirus Morphology.
abstract: MamaT was isolated from a soil sample collected adjacent to an irrigation canal in Pocatello, Idaho, USA. The bacteriophage has a podovirus morphology, infects Microbacterium foliorum NRRL B-24224, and has been grouped with bacteriophages in cluster GI based on sequence similarity. The genome size is 16,854 bp with 53.8% GC content. The annotation of the genome provides evidence for 23 putative protein-coding genes, of which 12 have predicted functions based on sequence and structure analysis. While MamaT has no tRNA genes, it appears to have a unique prohead packaging RNA (pRNA) system that includes a putative noncoding pRNA component.

title: Alternative splicing as a multilayered regulatory hub in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.
abstract: Alternative splicing is a crucial regulator of transcriptomic plasticity in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), and its dysregulation contributes to tumor progression, therapeutic resistance, and disease heterogeneity. While mutations in spliceosomal components or splice-site sequences can directly affect splicing, evidence increasingly suggests that aberrant splicing in PDAC results more often from the coordinated disruption of multiple regulatory layers. These layers include chromatin organization, transcriptional dynamics, epigenetic and epitranscriptomic mechanisms, and RNA-binding protein networks. Together, these interconnected processes reshape the transcript isoform landscape, producing oncogenic variants that facilitate tumor progression, metabolic adaptation, immune evasion, and therapeutic resistance. This review synthesizes the current knowledge on the multilayered regulation of alternative splicing in PDAC, distinguishing mechanisms that directly determine splice-site selection from those that act indirectly by regulating splicing factors, and from RNA regulatory layers that interact with, but can operate independently of, alternative splicing. Focusing on the dynamic interplay among co-transcriptional chromatin regulation, transcriptional kinetics, RNA modifications, and non-coding RNA-mediated regulatory networks, we examine how these mechanisms collectively remodel the splicing landscape to support tumor plasticity and malignant progression, while critically assessing the strength of PDAC-specific evidence and highlighting areas where mechanistic understanding remains incomplete. Additionally, we highlight emerging opportunities for isoform-level biomarker development and splicing-directed therapeutic strategies, while outlining the major challenges that must be addressed for their successful clinical translation.

title: Pneumocystis phosphoglucomutase links glucose-phosphate metabolism to β-1,3-glucan synthesis and cell-wall integrity.
abstract: The fungal cell wall is a dynamic, carbohydrate-rich structure whose composition is closely coordinated with cellular metabolism. Phosphoglucomutase (PGM) interconverts glucose-1- phosphate and glucose-6-phosphate, linking carbon metabolism with UDP-glucose-dependent cell-wall biosynthesis. We previously identified functional Pgm2 homologs from Pneumocystis jirovecii and Pneumocystis murina . Here, using a Saccharomyces cerevisiae pgm2 Δ complementation model, we examined the relationship between Pgm2 activity, β-1,3-glucan, and cell-wall integrity. Pgm2 deficiency reduced β-1,3-glucan content and altered zymolyase sensitivity without major changes in cell-wall thickness. Bulk RNA sequencing revealed that the pgm2 Δ mutant exhibited coordinated metabolic and cell-wall transcriptional responses, including increased SLT2/MPK1 , RLM1 , FKS2/GSC2 , GFA1 , CHS1 , CRH1 , SED1 , and CWP1 expression and decreased FKS1 , GAS1 , GAS3 , and CHS2 expression. Expression of either Pjpgm 2 or Pmpgm2 broadly shifted these responses toward wild-type levels. Selected transcriptional changes were further evaluated by qRT-PCR, which supported the major stress and cell-wall responses identified by RNA sequencing. FKS2/GSC2 showed the same directional pattern, although differences were not statistically significant by qRT-PCR. Despite this compensatory response, Pgm2-deficient cells were markedly more susceptible to sublethal caspofungin, whereas either Pneumocystis Pgm2 homolog restored tolerance toward wild-type levels. These findings link Pgm2-dependent glucose-phosphate metabolism with β-1,3-glucan levels and cell-wall function. Given the importance of β-1,3-glucan to the Pneumocystis cyst wall and its limited cell-wall biosynthetic pathways, these findings further support Pgm2 as an important component of Pneumocystis cell-wall biology and a potential antifungal target. Pneumocystis Pgm2 restores β-1,3-glucan cell wall phenotypes in Pgm2-defecient yeast. Pgm2 loss remodels the fungal cell-wall integrity transcriptional program. Pgm2 deficiency induces FKS2 and sensitizes yeast to caspofungin, a phenotype reversed by Pneumocystis Pgm2 homologs.

title: Network analysis of mouse brain proteomes resolves molecular and cellular endophenotypes of aging and Aβ pathology.
abstract: Aging and Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathology exert both shared and distinct effects on the brain, yet their relative contributions to molecular alterations remain poorly defined. Here we performed tandem mass tag proteomics across the lifespan in wild-type and 5xFAD mice and integrated these data with human brain proteomic networks to resolve aging- and amyloid-β (Aβ)-associated molecular programs. We quantified 8,535 proteins and identified 51 co-expression modules representing neuronal, mitochondrial, glial, vascular and proteostatic pathways. Aging emerged as the predominant driver of proteomic remodeling, with widespread alterations in RNA metabolism, protein translation, and neuronal pathways occurring independently of Aβ pathology. In contrast, Aβ selectively modified a subset of age-dependent processes, including suppression of mitochondrial ATP biosynthetic machinery and amplification of astrocytic and microglial activation states. These key aging and disease-related molecular signatures were highly conserved in human AD brain proteomes. Together, our findings establish aging as the primary determinant of brain proteome organization while revealing specific mechanisms through which Aβ pathology reshapes age-associated biological processes. Our results also highlight molecular mechanisms of human aging and AD pathology that can be modeled in mouse models.

title: Cytomegalovirus Infection in Human Cortical Organoids Induces Unique Developmental and Viral Substates.
abstract: Human Cytomegalovirus (HCMV) is a ubiquitous β-herpesvirus with exposure resulting in a life-long infection. Severe HCMV disease can occur in conditions of insufficient immunity, and this includes congenital infection. Infection of the developing brain can cause severe birth defects including microcephaly and sensorineural hearing loss. Also, increasing evidence suggests the contribution of HCMV infection in adult CNS diseases. Studying HCMV replication and its impact on CNS is restricted by host tropism and anatomy. In these studies, we define the impact of infection on healthy iPSC-derived cortical organoids using single cell RNA sequencing. We uncovered 16 cell type clusters in uninfected tissues using the Human Neural Organoid Cell Atlas. Following infection by HCMV expressing GFP, several clusters were altered in both GFP-positive and GFP-negative populations, including the likely transition of the Glutamatergic/GABAergic Neuron cluster into a CMV-Infected Cell cluster. Expressions of viral genes varied between cells and cell types, requiring us to introduce a TC (temporal class) indexing score to account for varying stages of infection. This analysis in conjunction with machine learning approaches revealed cells that are likely producing de novo HCMV along with several viral sub-states. Several viral sub-states had significant enrichments of genes involved in epithelial-to-mesenchymal (EMT) transition, including expression of EpCAM. We independently verified HCMV-induction of EpCAM protein expression in cortical organoids and glutamatergic neurons. In summary, our studies reveal unique features of HCMV infection of cortical organoid tissues, including varying viral sub-states and tropisms, and introduced new approaches to analyze these multi-dimensional complex data sets.

title: The Global Phosphorylation Landscape of Acute Heat Stress in Reef-Building Corals.
abstract: Warming oceans disrupt the coral-algal symbiosis that sustains reefs, yet the signaling mechanisms initiating bleaching remain poorly understood. Integrating global phosphoproteomics across three reef-building corals with protein structure modeling revealed conservation between coral and human kinases, enabling inference of coral kinase activities and uncovering a shared signaling program induced by acute heat stress. Heat rapidly activated ERK, JNK, and p38 MAP kinases, suppressed cell cycle signaling, and remodeled pathways controlling chromatin, RNA processing, and metabolism. Most strikingly, thermal stress rewired immune receptor signaling networks associated with non-self recognition, suggesting that heat shifts the coral host from tolerance to immune recognition of its algal symbionts. These findings define conserved signaling mechanisms that precede bleaching, revealing actionable molecular targets for enhancing coral resilience.

title: Quantitative imaging of native tissue architecture combined with deep multi-omics reveals the spatial biology of kidney aging.
abstract: Aging alters tissue architecture and metabolism in spatially heterogeneous ways, yet the connections between these measurable structural and compositional phenotypes and underlying molecular changes are largely unknown. Here, we introduce NORIGAMI (NoRI-Guided AI for Multimodal Integration), a pipeline combining Normalized Raman Imaging (NoRI), deep learning, quantitative morphology, deep proteomics, and metabolomics to investigate renal aging. Unlike conventional histology, NoRI provides label-free, scattering-corrected measurements of absolute total protein and lipid mass concentrations (mg/mL). In 32 male rats aged 9, 18, 21 and 25 months, NORIGAMI predicted the chronological age of held-out rats from NoRI images (mean absolute error 0.78 months; R² = 0.97), and whole-tissue images outperformed models trained on isolated tubules. Quantitative imaging identified 41 age-associated morphological and compositional features (FDR < 0.05), revealing anatomically heterogeneous and non-linear changes in lipid droplet concentration, droplet size, cytoplasmic lipid concentration and tubular architecture. Deep molecular profiling quantified 11,485 proteins and 269 metabolites, revealing coordinated declines in differentiated proximal tubule (PT) identity and oxidative metabolism, selective increases in basement-membrane collagen-IV chains, and increasing molecular heterogeneity with age. A protein clock, built mainly from extracellular-matrix and heparan-sulfate proteins, predicted age with a mean absolute error of 1.6 months. Old kidneys diverged along a dominant injury-remodeling axis, seen separately in the proteome, in kidney RNA from 54 other rats and in the metabolome, in which tubular-injury and immune proteins, including the NAD + -consuming enzyme CD38, rise as differentiated-tubule proteins and NAD + fall. NORIGAMI subsequently linked NAD + -associated molecular changes to candidate quantitative features of tubular geometry and protein-lipid organization in exploratory analyses, while complementary KIM-1-centered analyses identified overlapping candidate morphological associations involving epithelial injury and, possibly, lipid handling and yielded additional molecular candidates for mechanistic validation. Collectively, these findings suggest that declining tubular metabolic function, altered lipid organization and injury-associated molecular programs represent interconnected features of renal aging. NORIGAMI provides a framework for identifying the quantitative structural manifestations of molecular aging and generating spatially informed, experimentally testable hypotheses about tissue dysfunction.

title: Replication-coupled maturation of readthrough late transcripts by a polyomavirus small T antigen.
abstract: Productive polyomavirus gene expression requires the maturation of long, non-polyadenylated "wraparound" transcripts generated by late-strand readthrough of the polyadenylation signal on the circular genome, giving rise to structural protein mRNAs and microRNAs. In Merkel cell polyomavirus (MCV), small T (sT) antigen, along with large T (LT) antigen-mediated DNA replication, drives this process. Deletion of sT (MCVΔsT) attenuates late gene transcription, abolishes splicing, eliminates VP1 expression, and traps unspliced transcripts in the nucleus. Exogenous sT restored transcription and splicing in an aphidicolin-sensitive manner, requiring domains that activate DNA replication and bind chromatin. RNA sequencing revealed that sT promotes splicing and polyadenylation of wraparound transcripts, thereby increasing cytoplasmic VP1 and VP2 mRNA levels. A dual-fluorescence reporter confirmed that the leaky late poly(A) signal (LpA) was used more efficiently upon sT expression, indicating enhanced polyadenylation. Co-expression with LT abolished this effect, likely by overwhelming the capacity of the polyadenylation machinery. sT from HPyV7 and HPyV9 could similarly rescue this defect, indicating that this regulatory activity is conserved in a subset of sT proteins. Together, these findings define sT as a replication-coupled regulator of late transcript expression, splicing, and polyadenylation, revealing how a compact DNA virus converts readthrough transcription into productive gene expression.

title: SilencioM: silencing connected interfering oligonucleotides against MAPT as a potential disease modifying therapeutic for tauopathies.
abstract: Tauopathies are a diverse group of neurodegenerative diseases whose pathogenesis involves brain accumulation of misfolded, pathological tau (Microtubule Associated Protein Tau -MAPT-). More than twenty tauopathies have been identified thus far that collectively impact millions of people worldwide, of which the most common is Alzheimer's disease (AD). Despite substantial efforts to develop drugs for tauopathies, no effective treatments currently exist, highlighting the urgent need for therapeutics to combat these prevalent and ruinous neurodegenerative diseases. Strategies that target tau are likely to have the greatest impact since tau is the proximal cause of their pathogenesis. Small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) have emerged as a powerful class of precision therapeutics that silence disease-causing genes through RNA interference with favorable safety profiles. Delivery challenges are rapidly being addressed, and siRNA-based approaches are poised to transform the therapeutic landscape of neurological diseases. In this study, we describe SilencioM ( Silen cing c onnected interfering o ligonucleotides against M APT ) and show its efficacy in markedly reducing tau pathology after a single intracerebroventricular injection in PS19 mice, a mouse model of severe tauopathy. SilencioM targets human, primate, rat and mouse ortholog genes; thus, the same compound can proceed from efficacy studies to Investigational New Drug Application (IND)-enabling studies. SilencioM is simple to manufacture and is administered without encapsulation in lipid nanoparticles and without requirements for lipophilic conjugation, making it a promising candidate for further development as a novel therapeutic for tauopathies, including AD.

title: An ssRNA Phage Single-gene Lysis Protein Targeting MraY Reveals Convergent Evolution Across the RNA-DNA Phage Boundary.
abstract: Small lytic phages of the ssRNA Leviviricetes and ssDNA Microviricetes achieve host lysis by expression of a single protein, designated as an Sgl protein. Four ssRNA Sgls have been shown to inhibit steps in peptidoglycan biosynthesis: three target MurJ, the Lipid II flippase, and one targets MurA, the committed step of the pathway. A fifth Sgl, the E protein of the canonical ssDNA microvirus ϕX174, inhibits MraY, which catalyzes the synthesis of the first lipid-linked intermediate. This inhibition requires SlyD, a cytoplasmic FKBP-type peptidyl-prolyl cis-trans isomerase. The Sgl of the Caulobacter ssRNA phage ϕCb5 ( Cebevirus halophobicum ) has not been characterized. Here, we present physiological evidence that Sgl ϕCb5 targets MraY. Moreover, we show that, despite the absence of detectable sequence similarity, Sgl ϕCb5 shares several features with the ϕX174 E protein, including the distribution of hydrophobic and charged residues, a proposed N-out, C-in membrane topology, and retention of lytic activity in an Sgl ϕCb5 -LacZ fusion. Furthermore, expression of the Caulobacter cytoplasmic FKBP-type peptidyl-prolyl cis-trans isomerase CC2799 enhances Sgl ϕCb5 -mediated lysis in E. coli . These parallels between Sgl function in a DNA phage and an RNA phage either represent remarkably consonant convergent evolution or some evolutionary cross-over event for which there is currently no precedent.

title: Programming Primary Schwann Cells with Circular RNA Delivered by Listeria Drones.
abstract: Efficient transient genetic engineering of primary cells remains a major challenge in regenerative medicine, immunotherapy, and other cell-based therapies, as many therapeutically relevant cell types are refractory to conventional gene delivery. Primary Schwann cells (SCs) hold particular promise for peripheral nerve and spinal cord regeneration, yet nonviral gene delivery into these cells remains challenging. Here, we demonstrate transient programming of primary rat SCs using circular RNA (circRNA) delivered by attenuated, self-destructing Listeria monocytogenes ( Lm ) drones. These engineered bacteria invade mammalian cells, escape the phagosome, synthesize and circularize target RNA under inducible control, and undergo programmed lysis to release circRNA into the host cytosol for IRES-mediated protein synthesis. Previously validated in cancer and immune cell lines, this platform had not been evaluated in primary cells. Using a reporter nano-luciferase (NLuc)-encoding circRNA, we optimized SC bactofection across multiplicities of infection (MOIs). At MOIs of 10-20, bactofection efficiency reached 94%, with negligible SC death. Viable Lm were completely eliminated through programmed bacterial lysis and antibiotic treatment, yielding bacteria-free SCs that continued expressing the NLuc reporter for over five days and were suitable for transplantation. The platform enables straightforward replacement of NLuc with one or more therapeutic payloads. These findings establish the first demonstration of Lm drone-mediated circRNA delivery into primary cells. By enabling transient, non-integrating expression of therapeutic factors in difficult-to-transfect SCs, this approach offers a promising strategy for developing temporally controlled cell therapies for peripheral nerve and spinal cord repair.

title: AKAP-CaN-NFATc3 signaling drives persistent inhibitory long-term potentiation.
abstract: GABAergic inhibitory synaptic plasticity has critical roles in neuronal function, synaptic plasticity, and cognition. Activity-dependent alterations in gene expression are essential for generating long-term changes in inhibitory postsynaptic strength, yet the signaling mechanisms that drive inhibitory postsynaptic plasticity are not well understood. During an important form of inhibitory long-term potentiation (iLTP), NMDA receptor (NMDAR) activity promotes de novo synthesis of GABA A receptors (GABA A Rs) and the inhibitory scaffold, gephyrin, leading to persistent strengthening of inhibition. However, it remains unclear what activity-dependent signaling mechanisms control these changes in gene expression to maintain iLTP. In this study, we identify that activation of the transcription factor, nuclear-factor of activated T-cells (NFAT), and anchoring of the phosphatase, calcineurin (CaN), to A-kinase anchoring protein (AKAP79/150) are crucial in regulating long-term structural and functional GABAergic postsynaptic plasticity. Using short hairpin RNA (shRNA) to knock-down hippocampal NFAT isoform, NFATc3, we demonstrate its requirement for the synthesis of new inhibitory synaptic proteins, inhibitory synapse growth, and strengthening of synaptic currents during persistent iLTP. Additionally, using a knock-in mouse line containing a mutation in the CaN binding region of AKAP, we find that AKAP-CaN signaling lies upstream of NFATc3 activation and is required for increased inhibitory synapse clustering and synapse strengthening during iLTP via regulation of miRNA transcriptional activity and protein synthesis. Thus, we have identified an excitation-transcription coupling pathway that rapidly controls the synthesis of new inhibitory synaptic proteins and maintains persistent inhibitory synaptic plasticity, an essential process for memory formation and cognition in the brain.

title: Transcriptional and DNA Methylation Changes in the Hippocampus and Prefrontal Cortex after Fractionated Cranial Radiation in Mice.
abstract: Fractionated whole-brain irradiation is essential for treating brain tumors, but many long-term survivors develop cognitive decline whose molecular basis is poorly understood. We asked which cell types and gene programs change late after irradiation, how the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex compare, and whether DNA methylation changes affect the same genes or programs. Male and female mice received whole-brain irradiation (5 × 4 Gy) or anesthesia alone. Irradiated mice showed persistent deficits in executive function and spatial memory. Eleven weeks after irradiation, single-nucleus RNA sequencing and whole-genome bisulfite sequencing of pooled hippocampal (CA1-3) and prefrontal tissue showed cell-type-specific transcriptional changes in neurons of both regions. Both regions showed reduced ribosomal-protein gene expression and changes in adhesion genes, with reduced respiratory-chain genes in prefrontal neurons and bidirectional synaptic gene changes in hippocampus. Differentially methylated regions were enriched at promoters, with hypermethylation predominating in three of the four sex-by-region contrasts. Methylation and gene expression changes pointed to overlapping synaptic and signaling programs, largely through different genes.

title: Statement of Retraction: Long non-coding RNA lincRNA-erythroid prosurvival (EPS) alleviates cerebral ischemia/reperfusion injury by maintaining high-temperature requirement protein A1 (Htra1) stability through recruiting heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoprotein L (HNRNPL).
